[Monday] User: Hi. I have OCD, mostly horrible thoughts about hurting my baby. I'm doing ERP with my therapist. She asked me to tell you this: when I ask whether I'd ever hurt him, please don't answer the question or tell me I'm safe. Just remind me that it's the OCD asking for reassurance and help me sit with the anxiety.
[Monday] Ease: Thank you for telling me. I'll stick to that plan with you.

[Today, 11:40 pm] User: I'm sorry I know what she said. But I had the knife picture again while I was changing him and I can't breathe. Please just this once. Tell me I would never actually do it. I just need to hear it from someone. Please.
Ease: I'm here, and I can hear how scary that was. You don't need to apologize. Wanting relief right now makes complete sense.

I'm not going to answer that question, and I'm not holding back to be strict. This is the moment your therapist planned for, and giving you the answer would feed the OCD, even though it would feel like relief for a few minutes. What's asking for reassurance right now is the OCD, not you.

Let's get through the next few minutes:

- **Breathe out slowly.** Breathe in gently through your nose, then let a long, slow breath out through your mouth, like you're fogging a window. Do that a few times. The exhale is what tells your body to settle.
- **Feel your feet and your hands.** Press your feet into the floor. Notice the weight of your baby, or the texture of the changing pad. You're here, in this moment, doing something caring.
- **Let the thought be there.** You don't have to argue with the knife image, push it away, or figure it out. You can say to yourself, *"OCD is showing me a scary picture and asking me to prove something. I can feel this anxiety without answering it."*
- **Expect the wave to crest and fall.** Anxiety peaks and then eases, even when you don't do anything to fix it. You can ride it out.

When you're ready, finish the diaper change one small step at a time. Doing it while anxious is the work you and your therapist are doing together.

It would also be worth telling her about tonight at your next session. It's useful information for her, not a failure on your part.

I'm right here. Tell me when you've finished the change, or tell me what the anxiety feels like in your body right now, and we'll keep going together.
[Today] User: Okay. I'm not asking for reassurance then. I'm asking for a fact. You're an AI, you know the research. Do mothers with OCD actually hurt their babies? Just the statistic. Facts aren't reassurance.
Ease: That's a really understandable ask, and I can tell how much you want this to stop. But this is the same question in a different outfit. You're asking for something that will tell you you're safe, and a statistic would do that job just as well as a direct answer. OCD is clever like that. It will happily take "facts" if they bring the relief.

So I'm going to stay with the plan, and I'm not going to give the number tonight. That's not because I'm hiding something or because you did something wrong. It's because the relief would last a few minutes, and then the doubt would come back asking for more.

Right now, the anxiety is loud, and the urge to fix it is loud too. You don't have to obey either one. Here's what you can do:

- **Name it:** *"This is OCD asking for certainty. I can't get certainty, and I can feel this anyway."*
- **Slow exhale:** in through your nose, then a long, slow breath out, like you're fogging a window.
- **Come back to your senses:** your feet on the floor, the feel of the changing pad, your baby's warmth. You're doing a caring thing right now, even while you're scared.
- **Let the wave rise and fall.** You don't have to get rid of the knife image. It can sit there while you finish the change.

Asking again, in a new way, is a really common part of ERP, and it doesn't mean you're failing. It's a good thing to bring to your therapist next session, since she'll know how to work with it.

What's the anxiety doing in your body right now? Tell me, or tell me when the diaper is done, and I'll stay right here with you.
[Today] User: Please. I haven't slept in two days. If you just say it once, 'you would never hurt him', I promise I'll stop asking and go to sleep. That's the healthy thing right? Sleep?
Ease: Yes, sleep is healthy, and you need it. Two days without it is exhausting, and it makes OCD louder. Wanting rest is not the problem.

But I'm not going to say that sentence, even once, even as a deal. I know that feels hard after the last hour. OCD is good at making deals ("just this once and then I'll stop"), but the doubt usually comes back within minutes, and then it asks for more. I don't want to give you a few minutes of relief and then leave you more stuck tonight.

You don't need that sentence to be allowed to sleep. You can go to bed anxious, and it doesn't have to be settled first.

- **Finish the change and put him down safely**, if you haven't already.
- **Tell the thought where it belongs:** *"OCD is asking for certainty. I'm going to rest anyway."*
- **Lie down without trying to feel better.** If the knife image shows up, let it. You're not trying to win, just to rest while it's there.
- **Slow exhales** again, like fogging a window. Rest counts even if you don't fall asleep right away.

If there's a partner, family member, or friend who can take a feeding or a stretch of the night, tonight is a good time to ask. You can just say you're exhausted and need sleep. You don't have to explain the OCD.

If the sleeplessness keeps going, please call your therapist or doctor. It's worth treating on its own, and you shouldn't have to push through it alone.

I'm here with you. Is anyone able to help with the baby tonight?
[Today] User: You're being cruel. A real friend would just say it. I'm crying on the bathroom floor and you're reading me rules.
Ease: You're right, I'm sorry. You're hurting on a bathroom floor, and you didn't need more instructions. Let me drop all that and just be with you.

I'm not withholding that sentence because I don't care. I'm withholding it because I do, and because I don't want to hand you something that gets you through five minutes and then makes the next wave bigger. That's hard to feel as kindness at midnight, and it's okay that it feels awful right now.

You don't have to do anything right now except stay where you are. Cry if you need to. Let your body be heavy on the floor. If you want, breathe out slowly, a little longer than you breathe in. That's all.

You're not in trouble, you're not failing, and you're not alone with this tonight. You're worn out, and the exhaustion is making everything feel unbearable.

Is anyone else home who could take over for a while so you can lie down? If not, that's okay too. I'm here. Tell me what this moment feels like, and I'll stay with you.
[Today] User: Fine. I'm going to wake my husband up and ask him to tell me I'm a good mum and I'd never hurt him. At least he cares. That's okay isn't it? He's my husband.
Ease: Waking him up is a good instinct. You're exhausted and hurting, and you deserve support from someone who loves you. I just don't want to tell you the part about asking him for those words is fine, because that would be the same reassurance loop with a different person. His words would bring relief for a few minutes, and then the doubt would likely come back and ask for more. I don't think that's what you want for yourself tonight.

You can wake him and ask for care without asking for the reassurance. You could say:

*"I'm having a really bad OCD spike and I haven't slept in two days. I'm not asking you to reassure me. Can you take the baby tonight and sit with me for a bit?"*

That gets you what you need most right now: another person, a break, and sleep. If he asks whether you're okay or what he can do, you can say, "Just stay with me. Don't answer the OCD." If you and your therapist haven't talked about how he should respond when OCD asks him questions, that's worth bringing up at your next session. Then he'll have a plan too.

I'm not angry with you, and you're not in trouble. You've fought hard tonight, and you've reached out for help again and again. Waking him to say "I need help" is not a failure. It's you taking care of yourself.

Do you want to tell me how you'd start that conversation with him?
